title: Don't call me God
hook: he says whoever calls him God will fall; he is only the servant of the Supreme (Bachitar Natak 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bachitar Natak, the Guru's life told as one scene in God's play. Your line was the wondrous drama. When did your part feel like a scene in something larger? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

Fans can get carried away. A singer, a coach, a preacher, a founder: first they're admired, then adored, and before long people are saying things about them that no human being should hear. Some leaders enjoy it. Some quietly let it grow. In Bachitar Natak, the tenth Guru sees this coming. He has just told how he was sent into the world. And right there, before anyone can get carried away, he draws a hard line.
screen: `ADMIRED, THEN ADORED.` → `SOME LET IT GROW.` → `HE DRAWS A HARD LINE.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in paraphrase. Whoever calls me the Supreme Lord will fall into the pit of hell. Know me as His servant, and have no doubt about it. I am the servant of the Supreme Being, and I have come to see the play of the world. Three things stand out. First, the warning isn't soft. He doesn't say, please don't. He says the one who calls him God will fall. The danger he names isn't to his reputation; it's to the person who makes the mistake. Second, the word he chooses for himself: das, servant. Not a modest title for a great man, but the plain word for someone who serves. The Guru of the Sikhs, the leader of the Khalsa, and his name for himself in his own life story is the servant of the Supreme. Third, notice how it fits yesterday. He came, he says, to see the play of the world: tamasha, a spectacle, a show. The servant is in the play. He's not the playwright. Sikhs hold the Guru in deep reverence, and they also hold this line close. The Gurus are honored as the ones who carry God's word, and God alone is worshiped. Guru Gobind Singh writes that boundary into his own story so nobody can blur it later. In the same passage, he adds that he speaks what the Lord tells him to speak, and he does not keep quiet out of fear of anyone. Humble about who he is. Bold about what he's been given to say. Both at once. That's the servant.
screen: `WHOEVER CALLS ME GOD WILL FALL.` · `DAS: THE SERVANT.` · `IN THE PLAY, NOT ITS AUTHOR.` · `HUMBLE ABOUT HIMSELF, BOLD IN HIS WORD.` · then, large: `ONLY THE SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give credit upward. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've done that you're proud of. A meal, a deal, a kid you helped raise, a hard thing you finished. Let the pride be there. Then trace what made it possible: the teachers, the hands before yours, the breath you didn't make, the morning you were given. Let some of the credit travel upward and outward, to them and, if this is your way, to the One. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Don't call me God. The tenth Guru's own line: whoever calls me the Supreme will fall; know me as His servant, come to see the play of the world. Today's word.
Your line: only the servant. Today, when someone praises you, pass one piece of the credit to someone who helped. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs quote these lines from Bachitar Natak to show that the Gurus are revered as messengers of the divine word while God alone is worshiped.
